title: Understanding Workflow Artifacts
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of understanding workflow artifacts and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to understanding workflow artifacts.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on understanding workflow artifacts. Workflow artifacts are files retained from a run so that reports, packages, or build outputs can be downloaded or consumed by later jobs. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding Workflow Artifacts matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Workflow artifacts are files retained from a run so that reports, packages, or build outputs can be downloaded or consumed by later jobs. Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflow artifacts are files retained from a run so that reports, packages, or build outputs can be downloaded or consumed by later jobs. Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Logs and diagnostic bundles
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Artifact storage and retention
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - name: Create report
    run: |
      mkdir -p output
      printf 'validation=passed\n' > output/report.txt
  - name: Upload report
    uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
    with:
      name: validation-report
      path: output/report.txt
      retention-days: 7
content_blocks.expected_output: The run produces a `validation-report` artifact containing `output/report.txt` with a seven-day retention period.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use this in a workflow that can run on a test branch. Never include credentials, environment dumps, or sensitive test data in the report.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and remove temporary workflow changes. If you triggered a real run, inspect the run log before editing the file again.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain understanding workflow artifacts, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose between short-lived outputs, persisted artifacts, and reusable dependency caches.

content.task: Apply understanding workflow artifacts to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Workflow artifacts are files retained from a run so that reports, packages, or build outputs can be downloaded or consumed by later jobs. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Workflow artifacts are files retained from a run so that reports, packages, or build outputs can be downloaded or consumed by later jobs.
Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets.
